title: Acute short-term financial hardship can reduce turnout among poor German voters
source_unit: German individual survey respondents and elections observed under long-month-after-short bank-calendar timing
geography: Germany; comparative mechanism, not a United States estimate

observations.period: German surveys since the 1990s; individual turnout-intention results

denominator.unit: more than three million individuals across several large-scale opinion surveys

poor_end_month_turnout_intention_effect.unit: approximately percentage-point effect on turnout intention among poor respondents interviewed toward the end of an LMAS month

poor_turnout_intention_range.unit: upper-end percentage-point reduction range for poor respondents under LMAS across included surveys; reported range approximately 1–5 points

observations.method: Natural-experiment design using the irregular interaction between German bank-working-day timing and monthly payment conventions: long-month-after-short months temporarily stretch the same income across a longer interval. Survey regressions and robustness checks estimate effects on turnout intentions, with qualitative interviews used to examine mechanisms.
observations.uncertainty: The design identifies a Germany-specific, short-duration income-timing mechanism and the article reports heterogeneous effects concentrated among poor and working-poor respondents. The study does not establish the same magnitude in the United States, nor does it close a household remedy, attribution, or long-term political-action pathway.
observations.subgroup: Poor respondents, especially working-poor respondents and poor respondents interviewed near the end of the month; effects differ by partnership, inequality, and election context.
observations.counterinterpretation: The timing instrument may operate through stress, liquidity, social contact, political efficacy, or other correlated end-of-month constraints; the qualitative and mechanism evidence is not a complete mediation estimate. Institutional membership can cushion the effect in some analyses.

denominator.unit: elections in the compiled German electoral-turnout dataset

all_elections_lmas_turnout_effect.unit: percentage-point turnout difference for elections held in LMAS versus non-LMAS conditions

late_month_elections_lmas_turnout_effect.unit: percentage-point turnout difference for elections held in the last week of an LMAS month

observations.method: Multilevel election-level comparison of turnout under LMAS versus non-LMAS timing, with election-level controls and separate analysis of elections near the end of the month.
observations.uncertainty: Election-level effects are not individual votes, and the ecological estimates do not identify which person abstained or why. The paper reports a narrower approximately four-point effect for major elections and notes contextual heterogeneity.
observations.subgroup: All compiled elections, end-of-month elections, and major elections; reported election counts and samples remain separate.
observations.counterinterpretation: Election scheduling, composition, local context, and broader time trends may contribute to election-level differences even with the study's design and controls; this result is not a universal poverty-turnout coefficient.

related_sources.claim: The article identifies a replication-data archive for its quantitative analyses.

boundary: This is a Germany-specific comparative causal mechanism: short-term bank-calendar-induced income scarcity reduced turnout intentions and election turnout, especially among poor respondents. It is not a United States estimate, does not measure trust change or a specific responsible actor, and does not observe remedy, recovery, switching, non-use, or durable political realignment.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: American Political Science Review article page downloaded and hashed; abstract, design, individual effects, election-level effects, subgroup, and transfer-boundary statements checked against the published article.
